properties.name: Cameron
properties.basis: No map held prints the name, so the point rests on the timetables and the ground. The Midland Terminal's tables of 1920 to 1948 put Cameron 5.3 miles beyond Gillett. Measured along the OpenStreetMap trace from Gillett, 5.3 miles falls on the loop at the head of Grassy Gulch (5.2 miles at its top), and the trace runs on about 2.0 miles from there to where it stops near Independence, against a printed 2.5 miles to that station. The lidar ground at the loop is 10,027 to 10,046 ft, against printed altitudes of 10,040 ft (Short Line, 1909) and 10,080 ft (Midland Terminal, 1920). The point is the top of the loop, where the Short Line's trace meets the Midland Terminal's bank: moved about 860 ft north-west from the rough point the place was started with. The station, the junction switch and the town are not located, so the error is put at 800 ft (judgement: 0.1 mile of timetable rounding plus the error of measuring along a trace). Rejected: the place where the two traces first come together, on Beaver Creek about 1.9 miles east. It is only 3.3 miles from Gillett along the trace, about 4 miles short of Independence, and the 1951 map's spot height near it is 9,844 ft. One web page pins Cameron there, without a source. Elevation is the 1 m lidar ground at the point.
properties.summary: Cameron was a station and small town of the Cripple Creek district at the head of Grassy Gulch, where the Midland Terminal Railway, climbing south from Gillett, swung round a loop towards Bull Hill and Victor, and where the Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District Railway (the Short Line) met it. The Midland Terminal's timetable of 14 July 1895 has no Cameron: it has Grassy, 19 miles from Divide, where Concord coaches met every train and took passengers to Cripple Creek 'in twenty minutes'. Its timetable of 26 September 1909 has Cameron Junction at 20 miles, and those of 1920 to 1948 have Cameron 46.6 miles from Colorado Springs, 5.3 beyond Gillett. The Short Line's timetable of 26 September 1909 lists Grassy and, 0.7 mile on, Cameron Junction, 39.5 miles from Colorado Springs; Poor's Manual of 1902 gives it a branch from Cameron to Victor of 5.13 miles. A book of 1903 says the Short Line's lines parted at Cameron: one to the right over Hoosier Pass to Cripple Creek, the other to the left through Pinnacle Park to Independence and Victor. Library catalogues and a web history, all secondary, say the place was first called Grassy (or Gassy), that a company bought the townsite in 1899 and laid out Cameron, and that the Woods Investment Company built Pinnacle Park beside it in 1900: a resort with a dancing pavilion, a merry-go-round and animal cages, lying on both sides of the two railways' parallel tracks with a footbridge between. The post office is listed from 10 April 1901 to 31 August 1909. A 1954 newspaper headline says only the bear pits remained. On the 1 m lidar the Midland Terminal's bench comes round the spur east of the flat and ends in a curved bank 5 to 7 ft high, the loop, at about 10,030 ft. A second bench runs beside it about 12 ft lower, and a third leaves the top of the loop westward at 10,040 ft; these fit the Short Line's line as OpenStreetMap traces it, but nothing on the ground says which railway built them. West and south of the loop the present gold mine's pits, roads and waste dumps have buried both lines. The depot, the town and Pinnacle Park have not been located. The Denver Public Library holds two Poley photographs of the stage at the Grassy depot of about 1895, views of Cameron and of Pinnacle Park of about 1900, and an Otto Perry view of a train near Cameron in February 1949; the Pikes Peak Library District holds a view of the park's footbridge.
open_questions: Grassy and Cameron: one spot or two? The catalogues and web history say Grassy was renamed Cameron. The Short Line's 1909 timetable lists both, 0.7 mile apart, so on that railway they were two stops. The Midland Terminal's 1895 table puts Grassy 4 miles past Gillett and its 1909 table puts Cameron Junction 6 miles past (whole miles, and the two tables do not agree on Gillett either: 15 and 14), which fits either the loop or a point up to a mile east of it. Where the Grassy depot of the 1895 photographs stood is not established.

The position rests on timetable miles measured along an OpenStreetMap trace, and on printed altitudes. No map or plat naming Cameron has been seen. Western Mining History's map link (38.7467, -105.0991) is about 1.9 miles east; it gives no source. A plat, a mine map of about 1903, or the USGS sheet south of 38 45 N (not held) would settle it.

How the two railways were joined: a crossing, a junction switch, or both; where the Short Line's Victor branch left; whether the two crests on the loop were two tracks. The ground does not show it. The 1903 book says the Short Line's Victor branch turned left at Cameron and ran through Pinnacle Park, so the branch and the park were on the south side, where the mine now is.
Which railway built the lower bench and the bench west of the loop. They are given to the Short Line on OpenStreetMap's tagging and a library caption.

The depot, the town's streets, Pinnacle Park and the Short Line power house named in the caption of DPL X-609: none located. The park is 'south of town' (web history) and astride the parallel tracks (library caption). Ground south and west of the loop is under the mine.

Dates, all secondary and unread at source: townsite bought and laid out 1899; park built 1900 by the Woods Investment Company (PPLD caption) or owned with the townsite by the Cameron Mines, Land and Tunnel Co. (DPL index card citing the Denver Times, 24 June 1900); Short Line track 'soon to be completed to Cameron' on 3 March 1901 and formally opened 27 March 1901 (DPL index cards). The web history's 'In 1892 a railroad depot was established here' is earlier than the railway and is not used.

Post office: Cameron 10 April 1901 to 31 August 1909 (Wikipedia's list). The same list closes a Teller County office called Touraine on the day Cameron's opened (16 November 1889 to 10 April 1901; the 1889 looks wrong), which suggests a renaming or a move, but that is a guess: where Touraine was is not known.
When Cameron's sidings and station went. The timetables print Cameron as a coupon and telegraph station in 1920 and still list it in March 1948.

Printed altitudes do not agree with each other or the ground: 10,040 ft (Short Line 1909), 10,080 ft (Midland Terminal 1920); the loop is 10,027 to 10,046 ft on the lidar. For Grassy the Short Line's mileage and altitude disagree by about 1,500 ft along the line.

Photographs: the Denver Public Library catalogue was searched by hand in a browser on 24 Nov 2026 with about 17 keyword combinations (Cameron with Teller, Colo, Cripple Creek, depot, Junction, Short Line, Midland Terminal, Perry, CRRM; Pinnacle Park; Grassy; Gassy), reading the first page of results each time, and the Pikes Peak Library District's with 7. 'Cameron Colo' returns 729 hits, mostly people named Cameron and Cameron's Cone, so the search is not exhaustive. No Colorado Railroad Museum item was found. The seven library copies were fetched and looked at on 24 Nov 2026 and are shown; nothing on the ground has yet been matched to a photograph. Also searched that day: Wikimedia Commons and the Library of Congress (no photograph of Cameron, Grassy or Pinnacle Park; one Library of Congress search failed). The 1901 Trans-Mississippi Commercial Congress programme on cripplecreekrailroads.com, said to have pictures of the park, could not be reached. The Cripple Creek District Museum holds views of the park (linked, not shown).

Not read: S. E. Poet, 'Story of Cameron, Colo.', Colorado Magazine 9 (September 1932), pp. 194-5; the Golden Crescent (Cameron's newspaper) of 8 December 1900; the Denver Times and Gazette articles the library indexes cite; the Victor Heritage Society's 2025 talk on Gillett and Cameron (held in video/, notes taken only for Gillett).

Rights: one catalogued photograph is of 1949 (Otto Perry) and is marked as a library copy that may be shown. That rests on the permission the owner reported, whose terms have not been seen; confirm it covers photographs still in copyright before it is fetched and shown.

properties.name: Cripple Creek
properties.basis: The point lies on Bennett Avenue near Second Street, in the street grid that the USGS plate surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 letters 'Cripple Creek'; that plate's streets fall on the present streets within about 15 m here (by eye against the 1 m lidar). It stands for the town, not for a station: the Midland Terminal depot is a separate record about 530 m east, at the end of Bennett Avenue.
properties.summary: Cripple Creek is the main town of the district. The Sanborn insurance maps of September 1900 and December 1908 show two railway stations. The Midland Terminal's depot, two storeys of brick on a stone basement, stands across the east end of Bennett Avenue beside the tracks; a sign on it reads 'C S & C C D and M T Ry Union Depot', so the Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District (the Short Line) used it too. It is the building that houses the Cripple Creek District Museum, which the Denver Public Library records as opening there in 1953. The Florence and Cripple Creek's narrow-gauge depot, a long frame building, stood on Xenia Street about 150 m south of Warren Avenue, on the same lots on both maps; nothing of it is visible on the ground now. Fourteen library photographs are held, of 1894 to 1969; four made after 1930 are linked only. The Denver library's catalogue dates the brick depot to 1896, and the museum gives 1895; neither date has been checked.
open_questions: The Florence and Cripple Creek depot rests on two Sanborn sheets placed on the present streets by counting lots; nothing of it shows on the ground. The 1903 USGS plate draws tracks ending about 120 m further north, near Warren Avenue and Xenia Street, and no depot: not reconciled. Sanborn 1908 sheet 22 (its freight depot) and 23 were not read.
When the Short Line began to use the Midland Terminal depot, and whether the Florence and Cripple Creek ever did (the Denver cataloguer says so; the sign in X-744 does not), is not established.
The depot's building date (1895 or 1896 in secondary sources) has not been checked against a period source. The Sanborn sheets show it from 1900.
The Short Line's own approach and any station of its own in Cripple Creek are not located; research/26 traces its main line only to the east edge of town.
The Midland Terminal wye in Poverty Gulch (Poley's P-1710, 1896), its engine house (RR-1371) and the yards are not located.
The tourist railway's ticket office is said, in sources not checked, to be a Midland Terminal depot from Anaconda and Bull Hill, moved here in 1968.

Photographs: the catalogue of research/26 plus page 2 of the Denver search 'Midland Terminal Cripple Creek' (40 of its 123 results read) and one Pikes Peak search. Not fetched: X-839 (1947, from the right of way south of the depot), Z-11102 (1949), X-847 (1969), and the town views P-669, P-275, X-814, X-879. Four fetched photographs were made after 1930 (X-745, RR-1371, X-746, and the undated postcard 537-101): link only until the owner decides.
The town itself (founding, the fires of 1896, incorporation) has not been researched: nothing about it is stated here.

properties.name: Divide
properties.basis: The point is the standing depot, moved from the modern crossroads (OpenStreetMap's village point) 0.42 mile west-south-west, because the depot is the railway place and its position is now established: a Google Maps listing and satellite picture put a single building of depot form here, on the side of US 24 and Highway 67 that drgw.net gives, within about 30 ft. That the building is the depot rests on secondary sources. The junction of the two railways was about 300 ft north-east of it. Elevation is the 1 m lidar ground at the point.
properties.summary: Divide is the town at the top of Ute Pass, where the Colorado Midland Railway crossed its summit on the way west from Colorado Springs and where the Midland Terminal Railway branched off south to the Cripple Creek district. Poor's Manual of 1887 says the Colorado Midland was finished 100 miles west from Colorado Springs by 1 July 1887, which takes in Divide, and Divide is a station in the Colorado Midland's public timetable of October 1888, 27.8 miles from Colorado Springs. The June 1895 timetable names it as the change for the Midland Terminal to Grassy and Cripple Creek, and the Midland Terminal's own tables count their miles from Divide (1895, 1909) and later from Colorado Springs, Divide being mile 26.9 (1920 to 1948, altitude printed 9,198 ft). Secondary sources say the station was first called Hayden's Divide, that the Midland Terminal was begun here in December 1893, that it took over the Colorado Midland's track east of Divide when that railway was given up in 1921 (a Gazette headline of 30 December 1921 reports the purchase), and that the last trains ran in 1949. The post office opened on 26 June 1889 (Wikipedia). The depot still stands south of US 24, about 0.4 mile east of the Highway 67 crossroads and next to the old junction; a 2025 newspaper article says it was built in 1886, burned a year later and was rebuilt in 1903, dates not yet checked against a primary record, and it is being restored. The 1894 and 1901 government maps draw the Colorado Midland climbing to the summit by a loop north of the wagon road, and the 1901 map draws a wye where the Midland Terminal leaves it. On the 1 m lidar the loop survives as a bench now used by Grandview Drive, the summit cut west of the crossroads is about 30 ft deep, and south of the junction the Midland Terminal's bank runs past the reservoir dam east of town and on along the creek. A straight cut beside the loop that the old maps do not show is unexplained. The junction and the wye are built over. The Denver Public Library holds a photograph of the earlier depot of about 1896 and Otto Perry's photographs of Midland Terminal trains near Divide in 1935 and 1949; a 1949 view by Ralph Hallock belongs to the Colorado Railroad Museum.
open_questions: The depot's dates: the Gazette (2025) says built 1886, burned a year later, rebuilt 1903; 1904 is also given. 1886 is before the Colorado Midland is said to have reached Divide (1887). Needs a primary record (railway records, a newspaper of 1903 or 1904, the county's designation).
Whether the standing building is on the site of the depot in the c.1896 photograph (DPL X-7727), and where the 1887 depot stood: not established.

Where the junction switch and the wye's legs lay: the 1901 map draws a wye but at 1:125,000; the ground is built over. A faint line south-east of the junction is too steep on today's ground for track and is not taken as a leg.
Water tank, coal, section house, sidings or yard at Divide: no source seen mentions them. The 1901 map shows building symbols near the junction but not what they were.

The straight cut west of the crossroads, south of the loop: OpenStreetMap tags it Colorado Midland, but neither old map shows it and it climbs about 3.4 per cent. A line change after 1901, a siding or a road?
When the loop went out of use, and when the Colorado Midland west of Divide was taken up (1918 stop, 1921 abandonment: the secondary sources differ).

Mileage from Colorado Springs: 27.8 in the Colorado Midland's timetable of October 1888, 26.9 in the Midland Terminal's of 1920 to 1948, 27.4 on drgw.net. The difference may be a line change (the loop given up?) or a different measuring point; not resolved.

Altitude: the Midland Terminal timetables print 9,198 ft for Divide; the 1 m lidar ground is 9,112 ft at the depot and at most about 9,174 ft anywhere on the line inside the box (at the summit cut). Which point the 9,198 refers to is not known.
The depot is not in a timetable as a building; the timetables show only that Divide was a telegraph station from 1893 (a coupon station 1935 to 1940).
The 1894 and 1901 maps draw the loop about 800 ft east of where it lies on the ground; read only shapes from them here.

Photographs: the Denver Public Library and Pikes Peak Library District catalogues were searched by hand on 24 Nov 2026 with about eight keyword combinations (Divide with Midland, depot, station, train, Teller, Midland Terminal). DPL's search does not match phrases and 'Divide' is drowned by the Continental Divide (9,790 hits), so the search is not exhaustive. Where Perry's and Hallock's 'near Divide' views were taken has not been worked out. The library display copies of 13 were fetched and are shown; the Hallock view (Colorado Railroad Museum) and PPLD 103-717 (probably not this Divide) are not.
Newspapers indexed by PPLD and not yet read: Gazette 30 Dec 1921 (Midland Terminal buys the track as far as Divide) and 23 May 1976 (the depot renovated).

Rights: eight of the photographs shown are Otto Perry's of 1935 and 1949, held by the Denver Public Library. They are shown on the owner's instruction of 24 Nov 2026, under the library permission the owner reported on 23 Nov; the terms of that permission have not been seen, so whether it covers photographs still in copyright is unconfirmed.

properties.name: Gillett
properties.basis: Platted townsite; position from three registered insurance sheets and 2024 lidar.
properties.summary: A Midland Terminal Railway town in Teller County, Colorado, platted in 1894 on the flats north-east of Cripple Creek. It peaked about 1896 to 1897, held the bullfight of August 1895 in a timber ring inside its racetrack, and faded after 1900. Nothing stands today but the ruin of the Catholic church.
open_questions: Bull ring: position good to about 50 ft; the lens angle of the hill photograph (X-8601) is not settled.
5th Street photograph (X-8657): the standpoint is a guess and the building fronts do not fit the map.
Depot: the street side and the north end are conjecture.
Monte Carlo: orientation good only to about 20 degrees; wall height uncertain.
Catholic church: the north (rear) wall is not shown in any photograph.
Houses placed from the 1897 panorama on the far north-west slope may be 7 to 10 percent too near (evidence from three houses).
122 houses are illustrative placeholders: no photograph in hand gives their positions.
Which dam the 1965 flood photographs show.

properties.name: Midland
properties.basis: The point is the OpenStreetMap hamlet named Midland. It falls within about 300 ft of the building symbols beside the name Midland on the 1894 and 1901 USGS sheets, so the settlement's position is taken as measured to the accuracy of those maps. The railway grade, plain on the 1 m lidar, passes about 700 ft to the north-east. Where the station itself stood is not established. Elevation is the 3DEP ground at the point.
properties.summary: A small settlement in the valley between Divide and Gillett, and a station on the Midland Terminal Railway. It is in the public timetables from June 1895 (as a Midland Terminal station in the Colorado Midland's table) to March 1948, the last one read, at 6.2 miles from Divide in the tables of 1920 and after. Secondary sources say the first section of the railway was finished to Midland on 9 December 1893. The 1894 government map shows the name and a few buildings beside a road but no railway; the 1901 edition shows the railway passing east of the buildings and then swinging through a wide horseshoe curve to the south-east. The grade is still plain on the ground: a broad bench that bends at Midland and runs off along the hillside. The railway ran until 1949. People still live at Midland. No photograph of the place in railway days has been found yet.
open_questions: Where the station and any siding stood: not established. The 1 m lidar shows a level bench on the inside of the bend in the grade, about 700 ft north-east of the settlement, which would suit a station; that reading is a conjecture until a map, photograph or record confirms it.

Where the timetable's Midland was. Measured along the checked route, the settlement and the level bench at the bend are about 7.0 miles from Divide, which agrees with the 7 miles of the June 1895 table and the 7.1 miles Wikipedia gives. The Midland Terminal's tables of 1920 to 1948 print 6.2 miles (33.1 less 26.9), and that of 1909 prints 6; on the same route Gillett and Cameron come out within 0.2 mile of their printed figures. So either the later station stood about three quarters of a mile north of the settlement, or the later tables measure Midland differently. Not resolved, and it counts against reading the bench at the bend as the station of 1920 to 1948.

No photograph of Midland was found in a first search of the Denver Public Library catalogue on 24 Nov 2026. That search engine does not match phrases, so this is not proof there are none; the Pikes Peak Library District and local museums have not been searched.

How far Midland was from Divide, and when the rails reached it. The timetables give 6.2 miles (1920 to 1948), 6 miles (1909) and 7 miles (June 1895, whole miles from Denver). Wikipedia gives 7.1 miles and 9 December 1893 (citing L. I. Tingvik, 'Rail dates', 2006), and in the same article says the first narrow-gauge track was torn up in January 1893. The date needs a primary source.
'Founded 1893' is given by Wikipedia without a source. Whether Midland had a post office, and when, is not known here.
Elevation: 8,972 ft is the 3DEP ground at the point. The 9,407 ft in the Geographic Names record quoted by Wikipedia belongs to the census area, whose centre is about 0.8 mile to the south-east.
The 1951 and 1994 USGS maps at 1:24,000 have not been cut for Midland: it lies across the edge of two sheets.

Midland is missing from the Midland Terminal's own table of 14 July 1895, which lists only Divide, Gillett, Grassy, Independence and Victor; it appears in the Colorado Midland's table of June 1895. Whether it was then a regular stop is not known.

properties.name: Murphy
properties.basis: The point is where the printed mileage falls: 30.4 miles from Colorado Springs in the Midland Terminal's timetables of 1920 to 1945, that is 3.5 miles beyond Divide (26.9), measured along the atlas's checked route (as corrected by once_route_mt_murphy.py) stretched by 0.7 per cent to fit Divide and the Gillett depot (route mile 3.52). It has not been moved from that: no map held prints the name, and nothing on the ground says where a station stood. The ground does agree with it: the point falls within the one place along the bench between Divide and the summit where the formation widens (to 13 to 20 m, for about 330 ft: its own record), which would be the station ground if the widening was for the stop; that is a conjecture, so the error is not reduced. It lies on the old grade, which here is a side-hill bench seen on the 1 m lidar and named 'OLD RAILROAD GRADE' on the 1954 USGS sheet, so it is good across the track to about 20 ft; along the track it is good to about a quarter of a mile (0.1 mile of timetable rounding and 0.1 to 0.2 mile of route uncertainty: judgement, as for the other timetable pins). If Midland's 6.2 miles from Divide were taken to mean the settlement (6.86 route miles), the scale would change and the point would move about 0.35 mile south along the line, round the bend and over the summit; this is the larger risk and it runs one way. A newspaper of 1901 puts Murphy 'three miles south of Divide', which agrees within its rounding. Elevation is the ground at the point.
properties.summary: Murphy was a small station on the Midland Terminal Railway between Divide and Midland. The Midland Terminal's public timetables of September 1920 to January 1945 print it 30.4 miles from Colorado Springs (3.5 miles beyond Divide, 2.7 short of Midland), with no altitude and no telegraph or coupon sign; those of 1935 and 1940 mark its trains 'f', stops on signal. The 1909 table does not list it, nor does that of March 1948. It was older than the tables show: newspapers report a freight train derailed 'at Murphy' in June 1900, a passenger train running into the rear of a standing ore train 'at Murphy, three miles south of Divide' in August 1901, and hail 'at Murphy, a small station on the Midland Terminal road' in July 1907. At the printed mileage the old grade, named 'OLD RAILROAD GRADE' on the 1954 USGS map and now partly a trail in Mueller State Park, runs as a narrow side-hill bench up the west side of a valley; about 0.1 mile further on it swings round a sharp bend on a fill below Tracy Hill and passes through a cut over the summit of the line between Divide and Midland, about 9,390 ft on the lidar. At the printed mileage itself the bench widens, for about 330 ft, to a flat 13 to 20 m across, room for a second track or a loading ground; nowhere else between the highway and the summit does it widen for long. What the flat was, and what the stop served, are not known, and no map held prints the name.
open_questions: Where exactly the stop was. The point is the printed mileage only. Midland's own mileage is in dispute (6.2 printed against 6.86 to the settlement along the route); if 6.2 marks the settlement, Murphy falls about 0.35 mile further south, beyond the summit. The summit of the line (0.15 mile past the point) and the bend where a road came in on the 1954 map are the obvious candidates, but nothing confirms either.

Whether Murphy had a siding. The bench was measured across every 5 m from the highway to the summit cut: it reads mostly 4 to 12 m (the measure catches its shoulders), and widens only once for any length, to a flat 13 to 20 m across for about 330 ft at the printed mileage (record widened-flat). That is room for a second track a few cars long, or a loading ground, but too short for a passing siding for ore trains; the 1901 wreck, an ore train standing at Murphy run into from behind, does not need one. The 150 m past the pond, where a dam and basin have disturbed the ground, cannot be read. A railway track chart, a valuation map (Interstate Commerce Commission, about 1917 to 1920) or an employee timetable would settle it.

What Murphy served and why it was named: ranch, timber, ice, a section house, or simply the summit. No post office of the name is listed in Colorado (Wikipedia's list), no Murphy feature was found near here in a web search of gazetteer listings, and the library catalogues returned nothing. The 1954 sheet marks a well and three buildings near the grade; their use and date are not known.

The 1900 Victor Record calls Murphy 'the next station north of Gillett', which does not fit the later tables (Midland and, until 1933, Waters lie between). Midland had lost its post office in 1895; whether it was still a station in 1900 is not known.

When Murphy opened and closed. First seen in June 1900 (newspaper); printed in public timetables from September 1920 (no table between 1909 and 1920 is held) to January 1945; gone by March 1948. The September 1909 table, which lists only Midland between Divide and Gillett, omits it, although the 1907 newspaper calls it a station: public tables evidently left minor stops out.

The route through this stretch was corrected on 24 Nov 2026 at the owner's request (once_route_mt_murphy.py): between about 2.25 and 3.28 route miles it had lain on the creek's flat floor, with a kink, and now follows the bench west of the creek; that stretch and the bench on to the summit cut are graded measured. The route north of 2.25, on or beside the present highway, is still inferred: which side of the highway the rails ran is not settled.

Searches that found nothing (24 Nov 2026): Denver Public Library digital collections ('Murphy Midland Terminal', 'Murphy Divide Colo', 'Murphy siding railroad', 'Murphy Teller County', 'Place Names Colorado Murphy', 'Tracy Hill Teller', 'MT train Murphy', 'Perry MT train near Divide'; results are swamped by city directories and people called Murphy); Pikes Peak Library District ('Murphy Divide', 'Murphy Midland Terminal', 'Murphy Teller'; the only lead, photographs of a ranch homesteaded by a Patrick Murphy, is the Pettigrew Ranch on the Palmer Divide in El Paso County, not this place); Colorado Historic Newspapers ('Murphy siding', 'Murphy spur', 'Murphy switch', 'Murphy station' Divide: other places). Otto Perry's photographs 'near Divide' of January 1949 (DPL OP-12726 and others) have not been placed and may or may not show this stretch.
properties.notes: Started on 24 Nov 2026 from the timetable pin. The ground service (fetch_terrain.py) returned HTTP 502; the 1 m lidar box (3,600 m square, both surveys of the tile, nothing empty) replaced it. The Divide 7.5-minute sheets of 1954 and 1994 were fetched for this place; five other 1954 scans of that sheet are listed by the USGS and not held.

properties.name: Short Line Tunnel No. 4 (the Granite Tunnel)
properties.basis: Position of the bore from the OpenStreetMap trace of Gold Camp Road, which runs on the railway grade; to be checked against lidar. Identified as Tunnel No. 4 by its length: the trace is about 530 ft, and the Denver Public Library caption gives 521 ft for No. 4, the longest of the nine.
properties.summary: The longest of the nine tunnels on the Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District Railway, the Short Line, cut through granite without timbering: 521 ft. The line opened in April 1901 and was given up about 1920; its grade became a toll road and then Gold Camp Road. A curved timber trestle led to one portal.
open_questions: The McClure photograph (MCC-83) shows the south portal: its camera solves there to 12 px, and only that portal has a hollow for the trestle. The north portal was not put through the solver, because the ground there has no hollow at all. The camera is good only to about 150 ft.
The tunnel numbering: sources disagree on which tunnels survive and how they are numbered. No. 4 here rests on the length alone.
Dates of the line (opened April 1901, abandoned about 1920 to 1922) are from secondary sources and need a primary one.
The portals read off the lidar are about 440 ft apart, against 521 ft in the library caption and about 530 ft on the map trace; the approach cuts may hide the true portals.

The trestle carried from the photograph to the ground comes out about 500 ft long and up to 70 ft high, but its far end misses the grade by about 45 ft, so its course is good only to about 100 ft. A second photograph, or the trestle footings on the ground, would fix it.
The portal was taken as 16 ft wide and 19 ft from rail to crown to give the photograph its scale. That is an assumption, not a measurement; the bore still exists and could be measured.

properties.name: Victor
properties.basis: The point is OpenStreetMap's for the present town, in the middle of the street grid that the USGS maps surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 both letter 'Victor'; the 1903 map's streets fall on the present streets within about 15 m here (tested by eye against the 1 m lidar). It stands for the town, not for a station: the Midland Terminal's depot is a separate record, about 900 ft to the north.
properties.summary: Victor is the second town of the Cripple Creek district, on the south side of Battle Mountain. Three railways reached it. The Florence and Cripple Creek (3 ft gauge) lists it in its timetable of 2 June 1895, 5.7 miles before Cripple Creek. The Midland Terminal lists it in its timetable of 14 July 1895, 24 miles from Divide, and in every table read to March 1948; its brick depot at 4th Street and Granite Avenue is on the Sanborn sheets of 1900 and 1908, is photographed in the 1940s and was listed on the National Register in 1984. The Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District (the Short Line) lists it in 1909, 44.5 miles from Colorado Springs, at the end of a branch from Cameron that Poor's Manual of 1902 gives as 5.13 miles. The Sanborn sheets of 1896, 1900 and 1908 show the Midland Terminal's main track passing the north-west corner of the town and its depot on a leg lettered 'Switchback', so that trains reversed to reach it (read from the lettering and the track plan); in December 1896 a freight car served as the depot, and the brick depot is on the sheet of August 1900. The Florence and Cripple Creek ran through the town south of Diamond Avenue to its own frame depot west of 3rd Street. Ten library photographs are held, of 1895 to about 1955.
open_questions: Settled from the Sanborn sheets (24 Nov 2026): the brick depot's footprint and corner, and that it was built between December 1896 and August 1900, not in 1895. Whether it stands today has not been checked on the ground.

Poley's 'Midland Terminal, Victor' (P-973, 1895-1899) shows a clapboarded frame station building. The Sanborn sheet of December 1896 shows NO Midland Terminal building in the town, only a freight car used as its depot at 5th and Granite, and the brick depot is there by August 1900. So P-973 is either a frame depot built and replaced between 1897 and 1900 (no sheet of those years was read), the Florence and Cripple Creek's depot (plain frame in 1896, iron clad by 1900) under a wrong title, or another place. Narrowed, not settled.

The Pikes Peak postcard of about 1902 calls the brick depot 'Union Depot'. The Sanborn sheets do not show a shared depot: in 1900 the brick building is lettered 'M. T. Ry Depot' and in 1908 'Passenger Station' (the index: M. T. R. R.), and the Florence and Cripple Creek has its own depot in the same block, about 100 m south, in 1896, 1900 and 1908, on its own narrow-gauge track. The two railways were under common control from 1904 (Moody's, 1917), which might explain the name; that is a guess. Not settled.

The Midland Terminal's switchback: where its leg left the main track is west of the sheets and not located. On the present ground the main track at the sheet's edge is 29 m above the leg's west end, so the meeting point was well to the west, perhaps the timetables' 'Switchback' 1.1 miles before Victor. The join drawn on the map there is conjecture.
The last 0.6 mile of the Short Line's branch into Victor is not traced, and where the Florence and Cripple Creek and the Midland Terminal's 'main track' went east of Sanborn sheet 3 is not read.
'R. R. war in front of Strong mine' (1897): the library's explanation names a railway not yet built. What the event was is not established.
Dates of the town itself (platting, incorporation, the fire of 1899) have not been researched: nothing about them is stated here.

Photographs: found by 13 searches at Denver and 5 at Pikes Peak, first page of results each; not exhaustive. Two (X-546, X-547) were made after 1930; the owner decided on 24 November 2026 to show them. Not fetched: Otto Perry's 'MT depot' of 1935 (OP-12767), whose place is not established; a 1974 view of a station on Phantom Canyon Road that the library places at Alta Vista, 5 miles south (PPLD 002-3279).

properties.name: Short Line tunnel, sixth from Colorado Springs (probably No. 6); found on the lidar, said to be blasted shut
properties.basis: Not on any map held. Found on the lidar only: Counted along the line from Colorado Springs this is the sixth tunnel, at about 15.8 miles from Colorado Springs Yard by the timetable's reckoning. Counted this way the Granite Tunnel is the fourth, as its library caption numbers it, and nine are found, as that caption says. McClure's photographs at the Denver Public Library bear this out in part: his 'North from Tunnel 8' has the Duffields stop in view (the eighth found is 0.6 mile short of Duffields by the timetable), and the library's note to his 'Tunnels 8 and 6' says both were later blasted shut, which would explain why the sixth is on no map. But his 'Tunnels 8 and 9' shows the two close together and he calls No. 9 the last of nine, so the ninth is near the eighth and is not yet found; numbers after the fourth are probable, not settled. On the 1 m lidar the route passes under cover here for about 197 ft (up to 121 ft of ground above the grade line), from 38.74169, -104.90197 to 38.74128, -104.90153: the portals, to about 30 ft; the length is of ground more than 16 ft above the grade, so approach cuttings are not counted (atlas/tools/find_tunnels.py). On the ground: the owner's photographs of 13 June 2026, taken about 25 ft from the north-west portal found on the lidar, show a low hole under broken granite, choked with fallen rock: a tunnel is here and its mouth is shut, as the library's note says.
properties.summary: A tunnel on the Short Line, found on the lidar and seen on the ground with its mouth choked shut; sixth from Colorado Springs.

properties.name: Skaguay power plant (Pikes Peak Power Company), site
properties.basis: The 1951 USGS map draws a group of five buildings here on Beaver Creek, at about 7,800 ft, at the foot of a double-dashed line running straight down the slope from the north-west; it does not name them. On the 1 m lidar a level pad lies at this point (7,748 ft) at the foot of a dead-straight line cut up the slope for at least 1,400 ft. No other group of buildings was seen drawn in the canyon between here and the dam, 3.7 miles upstream in a straight line. That this is the Skaguay plant is inferred from those and from the accounts, which put the plant on Beaver Creek below Skaguay Reservoir, reached by a cable incline. Position from the lidar pad; the map's buildings, placed by the sheet's corner marks, fall within about 130 ft of it. Dates and figures here are from secondary accounts, not from a record the project has seen.
properties.summary: The hydro-electric plant of the Pikes Peak Power Company on Beaver Creek, said to have made power for Victor and the district from 1901 until a flood in June 1965. The site is inferred from a 1951 map and the lidar; nothing here has been worked up.

properties.name: Skaguay Dam and Reservoir
properties.basis: The dam as drawn and named on OpenStreetMap; the 1951 USGS map shows the reservoir and dam at the same place, and the lidar gives the crest at about 8,910 ft. The accounts say the dam was finished in 1901 and call it steel-faced and rock-filled. Dates and figures here are from secondary accounts, not from a record the project has seen.
properties.summary: The dam on West Beaver Creek that fed the Skaguay power plant through a wood-stave pipe. Pinned from the modern map.

properties.name: Skaguay pipeline: wood-stave pipe seen here
properties.basis: The owner's photographs of 3 July 2026 show a pipe of wooden staves bound with iron bands lying here, about 1,700 ft east-south-east of the dam and, by the lidar, about 100 ft below its crest (phone position, stated error 16 ft). That it is the power plant's supply pipe is the owner's identification and fits the accounts, which give a wood-stave line 23,200 ft long and 30 inches across, with a tunnel of 1,535 ft. This is the one point where the pipe itself has been seen. Its bed is traced from here on the lidar for about three miles (drawn as a dashed line); the last stretch to the plant, and the tunnel, are not located. Dates and figures here are from secondary accounts, not from a record the project has seen.
properties.summary: A surviving length of the wood-stave pipe that carried water from Skaguay Dam toward the power plant. The dashed line from here is its bed as traced on the lidar; the last stretch to the plant is not found.

properties.name: Platt Rogers Tunnel, lettered portal (west end)
properties.basis: The owner's photographs of 30 August 2026 show a concrete portal here lettered 'PLATT ROGERS TUNNEL 6100 FEET LONG 1952 BROADMOOR HOTEL WATER & POWER CO.' (phone position, stated error 15 ft). The name, length, date and builder are the inscription's; no written account of the tunnel has been found. The lidar gives the ground here as 9,818 ft and at the other end as 9,777 ft, so the water is taken to run from here eastward: inferred.
properties.summary: The west portal of a water tunnel built in 1952 for the Broadmoor Hotel Water and Power Company, by its own inscription. About 350 ft from the Short Line's old grade.

properties.name: Platt Rogers Tunnel, east end (inferred)
properties.basis: The owner's photographs of 30 August 2026 show a concrete headwall here at the head of a cut (phone position, stated error 7 ft). It stands 6,075 ft from the lettered portal, which fits the '6100 FEET LONG' lettered there, and 40 ft lower by the lidar; it carries no lettering in the photographs. Taken to be the tunnel's other end on those grounds. Penrose-Rosemont Reservoir lies 0.7 mile further east and about 95 ft lower; that the tunnel feeds it is a guess.
properties.summary: A concrete headwall taken to be the east end of the Platt Rogers water tunnel, by its distance from the lettered portal.
